subject: radiology
title: Cannonball Metastases, Egg Shell Calcification and Miliary Mottling

steps.title: Cannonball metastases are blood borne
steps.tx: **Cannonball metastases** are large, round, sharply edged lung nodules scattered through both lungs by tumour emboli travelling in pulmonary arteries. Renal cell carcinoma and choriocarcinoma classically throw these big smooth balls, while breast, thyroid and colon cancers seed smaller nodules more often. Lower lobes collect more deposits because they receive the greater share of pulmonary blood flow in the upright lung.

steps.tx: Tumour fragments carried in pulmonary arteries land as **cannonball metastases**, large round nodules with sharp edges in both lungs. Renal cell carcinoma and choriocarcinoma are the classic origins of these big smooth balls. Cancers of breast, thyroid and colon more often seed smaller nodules. In an upright patient the lower lobes receive more pulmonary blood flow than the upper lobes, so they usually collect more of the deposits. The pattern means blood borne spread, not a disease that was inhaled.

Renal cell carcinoma and choriocarcinoma classically make the biggest smooth balls. Breast, thyroid and colon cancers tend to make smaller nodules. Lower lobes gather more of them because they receive more blood flow when the patient is upright.

vis.alt: A frontal chest radiograph shows many large, round, sharply edged nodules scattered through both lungs.
vis.caption: Both lungs contain multiple large round nodules with crisp margins, more numerous toward the bases. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.title: Feeding vessel and smooth margins
steps.tx: **Feeding vessel sign** shows a pulmonary artery branch running straight into a nodule, supporting a blood borne origin on CT. Haematogenous metastases tend to grow smoother than the primary tumour that seeded them, with round margins and varied sizes reflecting repeated embolic showers. Head and neck squamous cancers break the smooth rule because their lung deposits cavitate often, leaving thick walled holes inside nodules.

steps.title: Finding the primary tumour
steps.tx: **Primary search** after cannonball nodules starts with kidneys, testes, thyroid, breast and colon because those sources dominate examination lists. A renal mass with lung balls points to clear cell carcinoma spreading through the renal vein and inferior vena cava. A testicular mass with very high human chorionic gonadotropin points to choriocarcinoma, whose lung deposits bleed and show haloes of haemorrhage around each nodule.

steps.title: Egg shell calcification in nodes
steps.tx: **Egg shell calcification** rims hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes with a thin calcified shell under 2 mm thick covering most of the node circumference. Silicosis in miners and stone workers is the classic cause, and only about 5 percent of silicotic nodes rim this way. Sarcoidosis, treated lymphoma and tuberculosis also rim nodes occasionally, so exposure history separates the occupational cause from its mimics.

steps.title: Miliary mottling means millet seeds
steps.tx: **Miliary mottling** covers both lungs with uniform nodules 1 to 3 mm wide, named after millet seeds. Miliary tuberculosis seeds them through the bloodstream during uncontrolled primary infection, in infants, malnourished patients and advanced HIV. The nodules share one size because one embolic shower seeded them together. Silicosis, metastases and sarcoidosis mimic the pattern but vary more in size or favour upper zones.

steps.tx: Nodules of one size, about 1 to 3 mm, spread through both lungs are **miliary mottling**, named for millet seeds. Miliary tuberculosis deposits them in one bloodstream shower while primary infection is uncontrolled, especially in infants, in malnutrition and in advanced HIV. Equal diameter is the clue that a single shower, not many separate events, seeded the lungs. Silicosis, metastatic carcinoma and sarcoidosis can look similar on the film, but their nodules usually vary in size or prefer the upper zones instead of a perfectly even field.
steps.say: Miliary mottling is a carpet of equal nodules 1 to 3 millimetres wide across both lungs, named after millet seeds. Tuberculosis plants them by blood during uncontrolled primary infection, particularly in infants, malnutrition and advanced HIV. Mimics such as silicosis, metastases and sarcoidosis usually vary in nodule size or favour the upper zones.

steps.title: Miliary tuberculosis workup
steps.tx: **Miliary tuberculosis** with a normal early film is common because nodules need weeks to reach visible size, so treatment starts on clinical suspicion in a deteriorating patient. Fundoscopy can show choroidal tubercles, and liver or bone marrow biopsy finds granulomas when sputum stays negative. HIV testing, sputum molecular testing and lumbar puncture for meningitis complete the first day screen because meningeal spread changes drug duration.

steps.title: Random versus perilymphatic nodules
steps.tx: **Random distribution** places miliary and metastatic nodules anywhere including fissure surfaces, because blood delivers them evenly through the lobule. Perilymphatic diseases like sarcoidosis and silicosis instead bead along bronchi, vessels, septa and fissures where lymphatics run. Centrilobular causes such as hypersensitivity pneumonitis spare the fissures entirely. Naming the lobular address on CT therefore narrows a page of causes to a short working list.

steps.title: Cannonballs versus septic emboli
steps.tx: **Septic emboli** mimic metastases with multiple peripheral nodules, but they evolve over days, cavitate early and arrive with fever, a heart murmur or an infected line. The feeding vessel sign appears in both, so it cannot separate them alone. Blood cultures, echocardiography and a hunt for endocarditis or an infected thrombus decide the path, while a known renal or testicular primary with slow growth favours true cannonball metastases.
